hook: Marcus, 17, collapses during football practice on a muggy August afternoon. His shirt is soaked and sweat is pouring off him, yet his temperature is 40 °C. The trainer moves him into the shade, strips off his gear and sprays him with water in front of a fan while a tub of ice water is filled, then lowers him into it. To see why he overheated while sweating so hard, and why water and moving air cool him, you need to know how your skin trades heat with the air.

prereq.q: In a negative feedback loop, what does the response do to the stimulus?
options: Opposes it, returning the variable toward the set point
prereq.why: In negative feedback, the response pushes the regulated variable back toward the set point, so the stimulus shrinks and the loop switches itself off.

prereq.q: What happens to blood flow into a tissue when the smooth muscle in the walls of its small arteries relaxes?
prereq.why: Relaxed smooth muscle lets the vessel widen (vasodilation). A wider vessel has less resistance, so more blood flows through.

prereq.q: Which layer of the epidermis is made of flat, dead, keratin-filled cells sealed by lipid sheets?
prereq.why: The stratum corneum is the surface layer of dead, keratin-filled cells in lipid sheets, and it is the core of the skin's barrier.

anatomy.caption: The skin's working parts: blood vessels, sweat glands and nerve endings in the dermis and hypodermis. Hide the labels and find the vessel networks, the eccrine sweat gland and the lamellated corpuscle.

chain.cause: Exercise raises heat production, and body temperature starts to rise.
chain.effect: Warm-sensitive nerve endings in the skin and temperature-sensitive neurons in the brain signal the brain's temperature control center.

chain.cause: The control center detects a temperature above its set point.
chain.effect: It sends nerve signals that widen the vessels of the dermis and make the eccrine sweat glands secrete.

chain.cause: Dermal blood flow rises and sweat spreads over the skin.
chain.effect: The skin surface warms and stays wet, so more heat is lost by radiation, convection and, above all, evaporation.

chain.cause: Heat loss now matches heat production.
chain.effect: Body temperature falls back toward the set point, the stimulus shrinks, and the responses ease off: negative feedback.

misconception.wrong: The more you sweat, the more you cool down.
misconception.right: Sweat cools you only when it evaporates: each liter that turns to vapor on your skin removes about 580 kcal, while sweat that drips off removes almost none. In humid air, sweat evaporates slowly, so a person can be dripping with sweat and still overheating. Fanning and misting help because moving air and a thin film of water speed evaporation.

summary: The skin is a barrier: dead, keratin-filled cells joined tightly and sealed by lipid sheets, on a dry, shed, slightly acidic surface, keep water in and microbes out, while lipid-soluble substances can slowly pass. Its touch receptors include free nerve endings (pain, temperature, itch), tactile cells, tactile corpuscles in the dermal papillae (light touch) and lamellated corpuscles deep in the dermis (pressure, vibration). Heat leaves by radiation, conduction, convection and evaporation, each down a gradient; when the air is hotter than the skin, only evaporation works, at about 580 kcal per liter. In the body temperature loop, the brain's temperature control center raises dermal blood flow and sweating when you are warm, and lowers dermal blood flow and starts shivering when you are cold. UVB turns 7-dehydrocholesterol in keratinocytes into vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol); the liver and then the kidneys activate it, and too little causes rickets in children.
